summary: For 11–12 year-olds, teach resultant (net) force as the single force equivalent to all forces on an object: a zero resultant means NO CHANGE in motion (stationary OR constant velocity), while a non-zero resultant causes acceleration in its own direction. Confront three stubborn errors — 'no resultant means stationary', 'bigger force means faster' (rather than changing motion faster), and reading the resultant as an extra arrow added to the forces rather than the equivalent that replaces them. A single force's direction is the direction of the CHANGE in motion, not automatically the direction of travel. Build vector addition collinear-first (along one line) before head-to-tail addition for non-collinear forces.
misconceptions: No resultant force means the object must be stationary (ignores constant velocity)
A bigger force makes an object go faster — conflating force with speed rather than with acceleration (rate of change)
The resultant is read as an extra/additional force acting on the body (Gunstone et al.)
The direction of the resultant equals the direction of motion (it should be the direction of CHANGE of motion)
Adding non-collinear vectors as scalars, or using a 'bisector' shortcut for the resultant direction
Motion implies a force in the direction of travel (the impetus backbone misconception)

activities.title: Force-arrow playground: balanced forces that keep gliding
steps: Set the crate moving steadily to the right. In this model horizontal friction is treated as negligible, so the only horizontal forces acting are the arrows you draw.
On the already-moving crate, place two equal and opposite horizontal force arrows and adjust their lengths so they are exactly balanced (zero resultant).
Predict what the already-moving crate will do BEFORE releasing: will it stop, slow down, or keep moving at the same speed? State your reasoning.
Observe the crate: with balanced forces (zero resultant) it keeps gliding to the right at a steady speed rather than stopping.

Now make the RIGHTWARD arrow longer than the leftward one, so the resultant points right — the same direction the crate is already moving — and watch it accelerate; keep that arrow stretched and notice its SPEED keeps climbing for as long as the unbalanced force acts along the motion.
View an overlay showing a single resultant arrow that REPLACES the separate arrows (not drawn in addition to them).

Switch to the non-collinear mode: this clears the previous motion and sets the crate at rest. Place two arrows at an angle, join them head-to-tail to build the resultant geometrically, then watch the crate accelerate from rest along that resultant direction.
activities.insight: A zero resultant means no change in motion — which includes continuing to move at a steady speed, not only being at rest. A sustained unbalanced resultant keeps changing the motion; when it points along the direction of travel the speed keeps climbing, showing that force governs CHANGE of motion rather than speed itself. The resultant is the single equivalent of the combined forces, and for non-collinear forces it is found by head-to-tail (vector) addition. This model assumes negligible horizontal friction, so the drawn arrows are the only horizontal forces.

activities.title: Combining forces and judging the direction of change
steps: Drag arrows head-to-tail (or along a number line for collinear cases) to construct the resultant, then draw or state its direction and size.
For collinear forces, calculate the resultant: e.g. 30 N right and 20 N left gives 10 N to the right.
Answer multiple-choice items on which way the resultant points for an object that is stated to be speeding up, slowing down, or turning, and justify the choice from the stated initial motion.
Categorise described situations as balanced (zero resultant, no change in motion) or unbalanced (non-zero resultant, motion changes).
Decide whether a zero resultant means there are no forces on the object, and explain.
activities.insight: Collinear forces combine by signed addition along the line; non-collinear forces need head-to-tail construction. The resultant points in the direction of the CHANGE in motion — which can be opposite to the current direction of travel when an object is slowing down. A zero resultant does not mean there are no forces; it means the forces balance.

activities.title: Tug-of-war predict–observe–explain
steps: Set up two students to pull a rope tied to a central marker; they will both pull hard and adjust until the marker holds still.
Before the pulling starts, predict: if both students pull hard and the marker is held still, what is the resultant on the marker? Does a big pull on each side mean a big resultant? Say WHY.
Observe that the marker can be held still even under large pulls, then explain in terms of the resultant why, while it stays still, the two pulls must be equal and opposite.
Discuss the skydiver case: during a steady (terminal-velocity) fall, state the resultant and whether she is moving.
Discuss a braking car that is still moving forwards: state which way the resultant points and why.
activities.insight: Large equal and opposite pulls still give a zero resultant; the size of the individual forces does not add up to a 'big leftover'. A zero resultant means no change in motion, so a steadily falling skydiver has a zero resultant yet is still moving, and a forwards-moving braking car has a backward resultant while still moving forwards.

activities.title: Free-body diagram reference with the resultant as equivalent
steps: Reveal, one at a time, the labelled forces on a chosen object (e.g. a book resting on a table, or a skydiver).
Identify each force's direction and relative size from its arrow.
Reveal the resultant drawn separately as the single equivalent arrow, and confirm it is NOT added alongside the individual forces.
State what a static diagram does and does not tell you: it fixes the force balance, but a zero resultant alone does not reveal whether the object is at rest or moving steadily.
activities.insight: A free-body diagram shows all forces as arrows; the resultant is their single equivalent, drawn on its own rather than as an extra arrow among the originals. For a supported object such as a book on a table, the downward weight and the upward support from the table balance. A static snapshot shows the force balance but not, by itself, whether a zero-resultant object is stationary or moving at constant velocity.

checkQuestion: A skydiver falls and, for a while, falls at a STEADY speed (terminal velocity) — not speeding up. Two forces act on her: her weight downwards and air resistance upwards. What is the resultant force on her during this steady fall — and is she moving?
checkAnswer: The resultant force is zero — weight down and air resistance up are equal and opposite, so they balance. She IS moving (falling fast), but at a steady speed: a zero resultant means no CHANGE in motion, which can be either stationary or constant velocity. A zero resultant does not mean stopped.
